advances: An elementary displacement union bound proves a uniform exponential reflection gain for an unbounded number of positive resource constraints. The range is \(k\le\epsilon n^{1/3}/(1+\log n)^{2/3}\), with explicit absolute constants. The proof reconstructs the simultaneous dual choice, fractional-coordinate bound, resource margins, decreasing-event association, conditional Laplace estimate, and original-support counting comparison. It requires no unproved simultaneous-slab theorem.

proof:
The set \(D\) is finite and nonempty: it contains zero, and the first positive row bounds each coordinate of every point of \(D\). If some \(R_r=0\), positivity of that row forces \(D=\{0\}\). Its reflection moment equals one. Since \(0<c<1\) and \(1<g<4\), the conclusion holds in this case. Assume henceforth that all \(R_r>0\).

We first choose all dual multipliers together. For \(s>0\), put \(\psi(s)=\tfrac13\log F(e^{-3s})\), \(\phi(s)=\max\{0,\psi(s)-\psi(h)\}\), and \(\phi(0)=+\infty\). Differentiating the positive exponential series for \(F(e^{-3s})\) gives \(\psi'(s)=-\mu(s)\) and \(\psi''(s)=3\operatorname{Var}_{Q_{e^{-s}}}(u)\ge0\). Thus \(\phi\) is convex, vanishes for \(s\ge h\), and diverges as \(s\downarrow0\).

Minimize on \(\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) the function
\[
\mathcal F(\lambda)=\lambda\cdot R+
\sum_{i=1}^n\phi\left(\sum_{r=1}^k\lambda_ra_{ri}\right).
\tag{2}
\]
Its value is finite at the first coordinate vector. A finite sublevel is bounded because \(\mathcal F(\lambda)\ge\lambda\cdot R\) and every \(R_r>0\). A minimizing subsequence therefore converges in the closed orthant. Divergence of \(\phi\) excludes a zero argument at the limit, and continuity at the positive arguments gives attainment. Fix a minimizer and put \(s_i=\sum_r\lambda_ra_{ri}>0\), \(\mu_i=\mu(s_i)\), and \(\Lambda=\lambda\cdot R\). In particular \(\lambda\ne0\); no coordinate law at rate zero is used.

There is a vector \(x\) with \(x_i=\mu_i\) if \(s_i<h\), \(x_i=0\) if \(s_i>h\), and \(0\le x_i\le\mu_i\) if \(s_i=h\), such that
\[
Ax\le R,\qquad \lambda_r(R_r-a_r\cdot x)=0\quad(1\le r\le k).
\tag{3}
\]
To prove this also at zero multipliers, let \(\mathcal X\) be the stated box of allowed \(x\), let \(G_0=\{R-Ax:x\in\mathcal X\}\), and let \(\mathcal Q\) be the closed cone whose coordinate \(r\) equals zero if \(\lambda_r>0\) and is nonnegative if \(\lambda_r=0\). Suppose that \(G_0\cap\mathcal Q\) is empty. The compact convex set \(G_0\) and closed convex cone \(\mathcal Q\) have a nearest pair \(g_0,u_0\) at positive distance. Put \(v=u_0-g_0\ne0\). Minimization along line segments implies \(v\cdot g\le v\cdot g_0\) for every \(g\in G_0\), and \(v\cdot u\ge v\cdot u_0\) for every \(u\in\mathcal Q\). Applying the latter inequality to \(u=0,2u_0\) gives \(v\cdot u_0=0\), so \(\max_{g\in G_0}v\cdot g\le-\|v\|^2<0\). The same inequality on the cone gives \(v_r\ge0\) whenever \(\lambda_r=0\). Consequently \(v\) is a feasible direction at \(\lambda\).

The directional derivative of (2) along \(v\) is \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}v\cdot(R-Ax)\). Indeed, for a tied coordinate it is \(\max\{0,-\mu_i\sum_rv_ra_{ri}\}\), and for untied coordinates it is the ordinary derivative. This derivative is strictly negative by the preceding separation, contradicting minimality. Thus \(G_0\cap\mathcal Q\ne\varnothing\), which proves (3).

Choose an extreme point of the nonempty compact polytope specified by (3) and the tie box. At most \(k\) tied coordinates can satisfy \(0<x_i<\mu_i\). Otherwise a nonzero vector supported on \(k+1\) such coordinates and annihilated by all \(k\) rows of \(A\) permits small perturbations in both directions, preserving the resource sums and box constraints, contradicting extremality. Define \(I_0=\{i:x_i=\mu_i\}\) and \(I_* =\{i:0<x_i<\mu_i\}\). It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
|I_*|&\le k,&\Lambda&=\sum_i s_ix_i,&
\sum_{i\in I_0}a_{ri}\mu_i&\le R_r,\\
s_i&\le h\quad(i\in I_0),&
s_i&\ge h\quad(i\notin I_0),&
\sum_{i\in I_*}s_ix_i&\le2k.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]
Here the equality for \(\Lambda\) is complementary slackness, and the final inequality uses (1).

Now use the resource-dependent displacement width \(B_k=2\sqrt k\) and the integer inflation factor \(\kappa_k=4096\lceil B_k\rceil\). These are new parameters; only the coordinate normalization above is taken from the predecessors. They satisfy
\[
B_k\ge1,\qquad 4096B_k\le\kappa_k\le12288\sqrt k.
\tag{5}
\]
The upper bound follows from \(\lceil2\sqrt k\rceil\le2\sqrt k+1\le3\sqrt k\).

If \(I_0\ne\varnothing\), set \(m=\min\{|I_0|,\lceil\kappa_k\sqrt n\rceil\}\). For each row \(r\), choose \(I_r\subset I_0\) consisting of the \(m\) largest values of \(a_{ri}\mu_i\), with arbitrary resolution of ties, and put \(I=\bigcup_{r=1}^kI_r\). If \(I_0=\varnothing\), put \(I=\varnothing\). In every case,
\[
|I|\le k(\kappa_k\sqrt n+1)\le12289k^{3/2}\sqrt n.
\tag{6}
\]
For \(i\in I_0\), put \(s_i'=\kappa_ks_i\) if \(i\in I\), and \(s_i'=s_i\) otherwise. Under an auxiliary product law \(Q\), let \(J_i\) have law \(Q_{e^{-s_i'}}\) for \(i\in I_0\), and let \(J_i=0\) deterministically for \(i\notin I_0\). This law is only a device for summing counts on the original support. Write \(\nu_i=\mathbb E_QJ_i\) on \(I_0\). From (1),
\[
\nu_i\le\frac{20}{\kappa_k}\mu_i\le\frac14\mu_i\quad(i\in I),\qquad
\mathbb E_QJ_i^2\le\frac7{(s_i')^2}\quad(i\in I_0).
\tag{7}
\]

For any nonnegative integer tuple \(j\), define \(\sigma_r(j)^2=\sum_i a_{ri}^2j_i(j_i+1)/3\), the variance of \(a_r\cdot V\) when the \(V_i\) are independent uniform integers in \(\{-j_i,\ldots,j_i\}\). If \(I_0\ne\varnothing\), put \(U_r=\sum_{i\in I_r}a_{ri}\mu_i>0\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_Q(a_r\cdot J)&\le\sum_{i\in I_0}a_{ri}\mu_i-\tfrac34U_r,\\
\operatorname{Var}_Q(a_r\cdot J),\quad\mathbb E_Q\sigma_r(J)^2
&\le\frac{1400U_r^2}{\kappa_k^2}
\le\frac{U_r^2}{(48B_k)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Here is the full variance estimate. The lower mean bound in (1) and the second moment bound in (7) show that either variance quantity is at most \(700\sum_{i\in I_0}(a_{ri}\mu_i)^2/(s_i'/s_i)^2\). For \(\mathbb E_Q\sigma_r(J)^2\), use \(J_i(J_i+1)\le2J_i^2\); its resulting coefficient is \(1400/3\le700\). The sum over \(I_r\) is at most \(U_r^2/\kappa_k^2\). If \(m<|I_0|\), every other \(a_{ri}\mu_i\le U_r/m\), so the remaining sum is at most \(nU_r^2/m^2\le U_r^2/\kappa_k^2\). If \(m=|I_0|\), that remainder is zero. Inflation on additional indices only decreases the estimate. Finally, \(1400\cdot48^2B_k^2\le\kappa_k^2\) by (5) and \(1400\cdot48^2\le4096^2\). The first line of (8) follows from the mean loss on \(I_r\) in (7).

For each row put \(G_r=\{a_r\cdot J+B_k\sigma_r(J)\le R_r\}\), and put \(G=\bigcap_{r=1}^kG_r\). Chebyshev's inequality for \(a_r\cdot J\), Markov's inequality for \(\sigma_r(J)^2\), and a union bound show that, with probability at least \(7/8\),
\[
a_r\cdot J\le\mathbb E_Q(a_r\cdot J)+4\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_Q(a_r\cdot J)},
\qquad \sigma_r(J)\le4\sqrt{\mathbb E_Q\sigma_r(J)^2}.
\]
Zero variance or zero expected squared variance makes its respective condition identical. Under these two conditions, the increase above the resource expectation is at most \((4+4B_k)U_r/(48B_k)\le U_r/6\), by (8). This is smaller than the reserved \(3U_r/4\); hence \(Q(G_r)\ge7/8\). If \(I_0=\varnothing\), then \(J=0\) and every \(G_r\) holds identically.

All the events \(G_r\) are decreasing in every coordinate, since their coefficients are positive and \(j_i(j_i+1)\) is increasing on the nonnegative integers. Independent-coordinate laws positively associate decreasing events. To verify this directly, for decreasing bounded functions \(f,g\) of one variable and an independent copy \(X'\), the covariance is \(\tfrac12\mathbb E[(f(X)-f(X'))(g(X)-g(X'))]\ge0\). For a product of several independent variables, condition on all but the last variable. The conditional covariance is nonnegative by the one-variable assertion, and the conditional expectations are decreasing functions of the remaining variables. Induction, together with the conditional covariance identity, proves the product assertion. Apply it successively to the indicators of \(G_r\) and their intersections. Consequently
\[
Q(G)\ge(7/8)^k=e^{-dk},\qquad G\subseteq D.
\tag{9}
\]
The inclusion refers to the integer roots in the support of \(Q\).

We next control the loss of the original dual score upon conditioning on the possibly rare event \(G\). Put \(T=s\cdot J\) and \(M_Q=\mathbb E_QT\). By (4) and (7), dropping the fractional coordinates costs at most \(2k\), and changing each coordinate in \(I\) costs at most \(s_i\mu_i\le2\). Thus
\[
0\le\Lambda-M_Q\le2k+2|I|.
\tag{10}
\]
For \(u\ge0\), define \(\ell(u)=\log\mathbb E_Qe^{-u(T-M_Q)}\). Its second derivative is the variance of \(T\) under the corresponding exponential tilt. That tilt remains a product law, with rates \(s_i'+us_i/3\) on \(I_0\) and with the other coordinates deterministic zero. Therefore (1) gives
\[
\ell''(u)=\sum_{i\in I_0}s_i^2\operatorname{Var}_{Q_{e^{-(s_i'+us_i/3)}}}(J_i)
\le\sum_{i\in I_0}\frac{7s_i^2}{(s_i'+us_i/3)^2}\le7n.
\]
All derivatives exist because the rates are positive. Since \(\ell(0)=\ell'(0)=0\), integration proves \(\ell(u)\le7nu^2/2\).

Let \(D_G=-\log Q(G)\le dk\). Restriction of the expectation defining \(\ell(u)\) to \(G\), followed by conditional Jensen, gives \(\ell(u)\ge-D_G+u(M_Q-\mathbb E_Q[T\mid G])\). For \(D_G>0\), divide by \(u>0\) and minimize \(D_G/u+7nu/2\). For \(D_G=0\), let \(u\downarrow0\). Together with (10), this proves
\[
\mathbb E_Q[T\mid G]\ge\Lambda-2k-2|I|-\sqrt{14dnk}.
\tag{11}
\]

There is an unconditional elementary displacement bound at the chosen width. For any nonnegative integer \(j\), let the \(V_i\) be independent uniform integers in \(\{-j_i,\ldots,j_i\}\). Each \(a_r\cdot V\) has mean zero and variance \(\sigma_r(j)^2\). If this variance is positive, Chebyshev bounds the probability of \(|a_r\cdot V|>B_k\sigma_r(j)\) by \(1/B_k^2\). If it is zero, the condition holds identically. Thus a union bound gives
\[
\Pr\{|a_r\cdot V|\le B_k\sigma_r(j)\text{ for every }r\}
\ge1-\frac{k}{B_k^2}=\frac34.
\tag{12}
\]
For every root \(j\in G\), the endpoints \(j\pm V\) are nonnegative, and every displacement counted in (12) satisfies \(a_r\cdot(j\pm V)\le a_r\cdot j+|a_r\cdot V|\le R_r\). Both endpoints therefore belong to the original \(D\), and the actual oriented count obeys
\[
k_j\ge\frac34\prod_{i=1}^n(2j_i+1)\quad(j\in G).
\tag{13}
\]

We compare these counts to the original denominator. The nonnegative multipliers imply \(s\cdot z\le\Lambda\) for every \(z\in D\). Summing \(1\le e^\Lambda e^{-s\cdot z}\) and extending the sum to the orthant yields
\[
N_D\le e^\Lambda\prod_{i=1}^n(1-e^{-s_i})^{-1}.
\tag{14}
\]
Put \(Z_Q=\prod_{i\in I_0}F(e^{-3s_i'})\), with empty products equal to one. On the support of \(Q\), coordinates outside \(I_0\) are zero, so the exact product-law normalization gives
\[
\prod_i(2j_i+1)^2
=Z_QQ(J=j)e^{3\sum_{i\in I_0}s_i'j_i}
\ge Z_QQ(J=j)e^{3s\cdot j}.
\]
Square (13), sum over \(G\subseteq D\), use (14), and apply Jensen to \(e^{3T}\) conditional on \(G\). Then (9) and (11) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sum_{j\in D}k_j^2}{N_D^3}
&\ge\frac9{16}Z_Q\prod_i(1-e^{-s_i})^3
\,Q(G)e^{3(\mathbb E_Q[T\mid G]-\Lambda)}\\
&\ge\frac9{16}\exp\left[-(6+d)k-6|I|-3\sqrt{14dnk}\right]
Z_Q\prod_i(1-e^{-s_i})^3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
In particular the denominator throughout is the actual \(N_D^3\), not a normalization of a selected sublaw.

For \(i\in I_0\setminus I\), the coordinate factor in the last product of (15) is \((1-e^{-s_i})^3F(e^{-3s_i})\ge8/27\), by accepted fact `609407d6db81b18b`. For \(i\notin I_0\), it is \((1-e^{-s_i})^3\ge(1-e^{-h})^3=8/27\), by (4); this includes every Dirac coordinate, including dropped fractional coordinates. For \(i\in I\),
\[
\frac{F(e^{-3\kappa_ks_i})}{F(e^{-3s_i})}\ge\frac1{8\kappa_k^3}.
\tag{16}
\]
Indeed the numerator polynomial \(1+6z+z^2\) lies between 1 and 8 on \([0,1]\), and \(1-e^{-\kappa_kt}\le\kappa_k(1-e^{-t})\) for \(t>0\), by the geometric-sum identity for the positive integer \(\kappa_k\). Applying this with \(t=3s_i\) proves (16). Combining these coordinate factors with (15) gives
\[
\mathbb E_p\mathsf H_j^2
\ge\frac9{16}\exp\left[-b_k|I|-(6+d)k-3\sqrt{14dnk}\right]
\left(\frac8{27}\right)^n,
\qquad b_k=6+\log(8\kappa_k^3).
\tag{17}
\]

The remaining estimates are uniform in both dimensions. By (5), \(b_k\le b_0+\tfrac32\log k\le b_0(1+\log k)\), since \(b_0>6\) and \(k\ge1\). By (6), \(k\le k^{3/2}\sqrt n\), and \(\sqrt{nk}\le k^{3/2}\sqrt n\), the whole exponential price in (17) is at most \(Mk^{3/2}\sqrt n(1+\log k)\). Hence, for every \(n,k\ge1\) with positive capacities,
\[
\mathbb E_p\mathsf H_j^2\ge c\exp\left[-Mk^{3/2}\sqrt n(1+\log k)\right]
\left(\frac8{27}\right)^n.
\tag{18}
\]

Finally assume the range in the statement. Because \(\epsilon\le1\) and \(n\ge1\), this range implies \(k\le n^{1/3}\le n\). Consequently \(1+\log k\le1+\log n\), and
\[
Mk^{3/2}\sqrt n(1+\log k)
\le M\epsilon^{3/2}n\frac{1+\log k}{1+\log n}
\le\frac{\delta n}{2}.
\]
As \(8/27=e^\delta/4\), (18) is at least \(c e^{\delta n/2}4^{-n}=c g^n4^{-n}\), as claimed. All arguments also covered \(I_0=\varnothing\), the at most \(k\) fractional coordinates, every zero variance, and inactive dual multipliers. The zero-capacity cases were established at the start.
statement:
Let \(n,k\ge1\) be integers, let \(A=(a_{ri})\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{k\times n}\), and let \(R\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\). Write \(a_r\) for row \(r\) of \(A\), and set
\[
D=\{z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n:Az\le R\},\qquad
N_D=\#D,\qquad p(j)=N_D^{-1}\quad(j\in D).
\]
For \(j\in D\), let \(k_j=\#\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:j+v,j-v\in D\}\) and \(\mathsf H_j=k_j/N_D\). These are exactly the oriented reflected count, including zero displacement, and uniform-law overlap of accepted fact `3aa03555ebd91f71`, here on the stated \(k\)-resource set \(D\). Equivalently \(k_j=\#(D\cap(2j-D))\).

All logarithms are natural. Define the following absolute constants:
\[
\begin{aligned}
d&=\log(8/7),& \delta&=\log(32/27),\\
b_0&=6+\log(8\cdot12288^3),&
M&=12289b_0+6+d+3\sqrt{14d},\\
\epsilon&=\min\left\{1,\left(\frac{\delta}{2M}\right)^{2/3}\right\},&
c&=\frac9{16},\qquad g=e^{\delta/2}=\sqrt{32/27}>1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Whenever \(1\le k\le\epsilon n^{1/3}/(1+\log n)^{2/3}\), the original uniform law satisfies
\[
\mathbb E_{j\sim p}\mathsf H_j^2
=\frac{\sum_{j\in D}k_j^2}{N_D^3}
\ge c g^n4^{-n}.
\]
In particular this includes positive integer resource coefficients, zero capacities, inactive dual multipliers, and deterministic auxiliary coordinates. The constants are independent of \(n,k,A,R\).

The only coordinate facts used from accepted predecessors are these, in their exact normalization. Put
\[
F(z)=\frac{1+6z+z^2}{(1-z)^3},\qquad
Q_{e^{-s}}(u)=\frac{(2u+1)^2e^{-3su}}{F(e^{-3s})}\quad(u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}),\qquad
\mu(s)=\mathbb E_{Q_{e^{-s}}}u.
\]
Here \(u\) is the coordinate index, rather than the resource count \(k\). Accepted fact `609407d6db81b18b` gives \((1-e^{-s})^3F(e^{-3s})\ge8/27\) for \(s>0\); accepted fact `3aa03555ebd91f71` gives
\[
\mu(s)\le\frac2s,\qquad
\mathbb E_{Q_{e^{-s}}}u^2\le\frac7{s^2}\quad(s>0),\qquad
\mu(s)\ge\frac1{10s}\quad(0<s\le h),\qquad h=\log3.
\tag{1}
\]
No multi-resource conclusion is taken from either predecessor.
